definitions.definition: The science in which the wholesome and unwholesome, happy and unhappy life, what is good and bad for life, and its measure are taught (Ca Sū 1.41); so called because in it life is found or by it one attains life (Su Sū 1.15); it makes life known by its own marks (Ca Sū 30.23). It is beginningless and eternal (Ca Sū 30.27), an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6). Synonyms: śākhā, vidyā, sūtra, jñāna, śāstra, lakṣaṇa, tantra (Ca Sū 30.31).

The union of body, senses, mind and self; its synonyms are dhāri, jīvita, nityaga and anubandha (Ca Sū 1.42); the continuance of consciousness (Sū 30.22); fourfold as happy or unhappy, wholesome or unwholesome (Sū 1.41, 30.24); in Śārṅgadhara the union of body and breath (Pūrva 5.52).

The eight branches: kāyacikitsā, śālākya, śalya, viṣa/agada, bhūtavidyā, kaumārabhṛtya, rasāyana, vājīkaraṇa (Ca Sū 30.28; Su Sū 1.7; AHS Sū 1.5: body, child, seizers, above the clavicle, surgery, fangs, old age, virility).
Internal medicine: diseases affecting the whole body such as fever, bleeding disorders, consumption, insanity, epilepsy, skin disease, urinary disorders and diarrhoea (Su Sū 1.8).
Treatment of diseases above the collar-bone — ear, eye, mouth, nose (Su Sū 1.8); 'ūrdhvāṅga' in AHS Sū 1.5.
Surgery: removal of foreign bodies and management of wounds with instruments, knives, caustics and fire; the first and foremost limb for the Dhanvantari school (Su Sū 1.8, 1.17-18).
Toxicology: signs and treatment of bites of snakes, insects, spiders, rodents and of combined poisons (Su Sū 1.8); 'daṃṣṭrā' in AHS Sū 1.5.

The branch for those whose minds are seized by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, ancestors, piśācas, nāgas and grahas, treated by pacificatory rites and offerings (Su Sū 1.8); 'graha' in AHS Sū 1.5. Summary only.
Children's medicine: rearing of children, purification of the wet-nurse's milk, and diseases arising from bad milk and seizing spirits (Su Sū 1.8); the subject of the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā.

In Āyurveda the three bodily factors vāta, pitta and kapha, which balanced sustain the body and disturbed destroy it (AHS Sū 1.6-7; Ca Sū 1.57), and the two mental doṣas rajas and tamas (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21). Suśruta counts blood with them in origin, maintenance and dissolution (Su Sū 21.3-4).

cross_language.note: the three nyes pa of Tibetan medicine
Pali dosa usually 'hatred'; the humours are named individually (pitta, semha, vāta)

notes: Homonym: in Nyāya and Buddhism 'fault' (attachment, aversion, delusion).

definitions.definition: The doṣa of movement: dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear and rough (Ca Sū 1.59); fivefold as prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna; unprovoked it upholds the body's structure, impels all movement and guides the mind, and in the world upholds the earth and drives the seasons (Ca Sū 12.8); chief seat the colon (AHS Sū 12.1).

equivalents.note: vāta is vāyu as a bodily doṣa; Āyurveda uses vāyu, anila, māruta, samīraṇa as synonyms

definitions.definition: The doṣa of heat and transformation: slightly unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, flowing and pungent (Ca Sū 1.60); there is no fire in the body apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); fivefold as pācaka, rañjaka, sādhaka, ālocaka and bhrājaka (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-14).

literal: phlegm; also śleṣman 'that which embraces' (√śliṣ, Su Sū 21.5)

definitions.definition: The doṣa of cohesion and stability: heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, sweet, stable and slimy (Ca Sū 1.61); it upholds the body by the action of water — binding joints, lubrication, healing, strength and firmness (Su Sū 15.4); fivefold as avalambaka, kledaka, bodhaka, tarpaka and śleṣaka (AHS Sū 12.15-18).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the first of the five vāyus, seated in the head and moving in chest and throat, upholding intellect, heart, senses and mind and governing breathing, swallowing, spitting, sneezing and belching (AHS Sū 12.4-5); in Śārṅgadhara the breath that rises from the navel, touches the heart-lotus, drinks the nectar of the sky and returns to nourish the body (Pūrva 5.51); the 'prāṇas' also denote the seats of life (Ca Sū 29.3; Śā 7.9).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu seated in the chest, moving in nose, navel and throat, governing speech, effort, energy, strength, complexion and memory (AHS Sū 12.5-6).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu seated in the heart and moving swiftly through the whole body, governing movement, flexion, extension, blinking — nearly all the body's actions (AHS Sū 12.6-7).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu near the digestive fire, moving through the abdomen, which takes in, digests, separates and releases food (AHS Sū 12.8); it fans the belly-fire (Ca Ci 15.7).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the vāyu in the lower region (pelvis, bladder, genitals, thighs), governing the release of semen, menses, faeces, urine and the foetus (AHS Sū 12.9).
The pitta between the stomach and the intestine, which digests the four kinds of food and separates essence and waste and supports the other pittas; called 'fire' (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-12).
The pitta that colours rasa (into blood): in liver and spleen for Suśruta (Sū 21.10), in the stomach for Vāgbhaṭa (AHS Sū 12.13).
The pitta in the heart that accomplishes desired aims through intellect, intelligence and self-regard (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.13-14).
The pitta in the eye that makes sight possible (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.14).
The pitta in the skin that gives lustre (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.14).
The kapha in the chest that supports the trika and heart and the other seats of kapha (AHS Sū 12.15-16; Su Sū 21.14 describes the function without the name).
The kapha in the stomach that moistens and breaks down the mass of food (AHS Sū 12.16-17; Su Sū 21.12-14).
The kapha in the tongue that makes taste known (AHS Sū 12.17).
The kapha in the head that nourishes the senses (AHS Sū 12.17).
The kapha in the joints that binds them (AHS Sū 12.18).

The seven bodily tissues — rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow and semen — called 'the vitiable' (dūṣya) (AHS Sū 1.13); each is formed from the preceding by its own fire, with essence and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16); in Caraka's wider usage every body-constituent whose balance is health (Sū 1.53; 9.4); in Śā 1.16 the six 'dhātus' of the person are the five elements and consciousness.
The first tissue, the essence of digested food: gives satisfaction and pleasure and nourishes blood (Su Sū 15.5).
The second tissue: gives clarity of complexion, nourishes flesh and sustains life (Su Sū 15.5); counted with the doṣas by Suśruta (Sū 21.3-4).
The third tissue: gives bulk to the body and nourishes fat (Su Sū 15.5).
The fourth tissue: gives unctuousness, sweat and firmness and nourishes bone (Su Sū 15.5).
The fifth tissue: supports the body and nourishes marrow (Su Sū 15.5).
The sixth tissue: gives affection, unctuousness and strength, nourishes semen and fills the bones (Su Sū 15.5).
The seventh tissue, whose supreme essence is ojas (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); from it the embryo arises as its essence (Ca Ci 15.16).

Secondary products of the tissues: from rasa breast-milk and menstrual blood, from blood tendons and vessels, from flesh muscle-fat and the six layers of skin, from fat ligaments and joints (Ca Ci 15.17).

notes: Ref from the local Devanāgarī e-text of Ca Ci 15; the term 'upadhātu' itself is the later commentarial name.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the body's wastes — urine, faeces, sweat and the rest (AHS Sū 1.13); each tissue has its waste (Ca Ci 15.18-19); the doṣas when vitiating are also called malas.
The waste of food: gives support and holds wind and fire (Su Sū 15.5).
Fills the bladder and carries away moisture (Su Sū 15.5).
Moisture of the skin and its softness (Su Sū 15.5); the waste of fat (Ca Ci 15.18).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the digestive-metabolic fire; no fire in the body exists apart from pitta (Su Sū 21.9); life, complexion, strength, health, ojas, tejas and the prāṇas depend on it — extinguished one dies, balanced one lives long, disturbed one falls ill; 'agni is the root' (Ca Ci 15.3-4); its states are balanced, irregular (vāta), sharp (pitta) and weak (kapha) (AHS Sū 1.8); later counted as thirteen: the belly-fire, the five element-fires and the seven tissue-fires (Ca Ci 15.13-15).
The chief digestive fire in the abdomen, fanned by samāna, which cooks the food and on which the other fires depend (Ca Ci 15.6-8; AHS Sū 12.8, 12.11-12 as pācaka).
The five 'heats' of earth, water, fire, air and space that digest the corresponding elemental qualities of food (Ca Ci 15.13).
The seven fires by which each tissue is cooked, yielding essence (the next tissue) and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16).
The first tissue (rasa) left uncooked through weakness of the fire, vitiated and lodged in the stomach, is called āma (AHS Sū 13.25); it obstructs the channels and is the ground of many diseases.

notes: AHS Sū 13.25 checked in the DCS e-text; no teaching entry written for it.

definitions.definition: The supreme essence (tejas) of the tissues from rasa to semen, identical with strength (bala) (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); seated in the heart, pure, slightly reddish-yellow, ghee-coloured, sweet, smelling of parched rice, the first thing produced in the body, whose loss is death (Ca Sū 17.74-75); the 'supreme' (para) ojas in the heart as distinct from the ojas carried by the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.7-9, as the commentators read it).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) the fire element, the person's heat (Ca Śā 5.5); (2) 'essence' — ojas is the supreme tejas of the tissues (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); (3) listed with ojas, the fires and the prāṇas among what depends on the body's fire (Ca Ci 15.3).

notes: The grouping 'ojas, tejas and prāṇa' as a doctrinal triad is not found as such in the classical texts checked; Ca Ci 15.3 lists them among things dependent on agni.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the channels that carry the tissues undergoing transformation; there are as many as there are embodied kinds of things in the person; thirteen are named (of prāṇa, water, food, rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, urine, faeces, sweat), and for the mind the whole conscious body is its channel (Ca Vi 5.3-7); vitiated by excess flow, obstruction, knotting or wrong course (Vi 5.22).

notes: Homonym: in the Śaiva Mantramārga a 'stream' of revelation.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): called 'mahat' and 'artha'; the seat of consciousness, the self with its qualities, mind and its objects, of the supreme ojas and root of the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.3-7); the seat of consciousness and abode of ojas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.49); root of the channels of prāṇa and rasa (Ca Vi 5.6).

Ten seats where life resides: the temples, the three vital points (head, heart, bladder), throat, blood, semen, ojas and anus (Ca Sū 29.3); or head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh (Ca Śā 7.9).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one hundred and seven vital points of five kinds — of flesh (11), vessels (41), ligaments (27), bone (8) and joints (20) (Su Śā 6.3-4); the three great marmas are head, heart and bladder (Ca Sū 29.3). (Marma in depth: U58.)

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) bodily constitution — the doṣa predominating from conception, giving vāta-, pitta-, kapha-, mixed or balanced natures (Ca Sū 7.39-40; Vi 8.95; AHS Sū 1.9-10); (2) the normal state, i.e. balance of the dhātus (Ca Sū 9.4); (3) the eightfold prakṛti of the person's principles (Ca Śā 1.63); (4) for Suśruta 'in medicine' nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation are held to be the source (Su Śā 1.11).

The morbid state of the patient, examined second in the tenfold examination (Ca Vi 8.94); the deviations from normal that signal disease or approaching death (Ca In 1.6-7); disorder as imbalance of the dhātus (Sū 9.4).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka a name of the mind, one leg of the tripod of life (Sū 1.46; Vi 8.119); the mind named after the quality that predominates (Sū 8.6); the pure (śuddha) mind as against the rājasa and tāmasa (Śā 4.36); of superior, middling or inferior strength (Vi 8.119).

equivalents.note: in Caraka's usage sattva, cetas and manas name the mind

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): with tamas one of the two doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; AHS Sū 1.21); the rājasa mind is faulty, having the part of anger (Śā 4.36); rajas and tamas bind the person to the wheel of births (Śā 1.36, 1.68); their absence is a condition of liberation (Śā 1.142).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the second doṣa of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57); the tāmasa mind has the part of delusion (Śā 4.36); sleep born of tamas is the root of sin (Sū 21.59).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): beyond the senses, called sattva or cetas; one in number though it seems many; the senses grasp objects only when led by it (Ca Sū 8.4-7); its marks are the presence or absence of knowledge, its qualities atomicity and oneness, its objects what is thought, considered, reasoned, meditated and resolved, its acts directing the senses and restraining itself (Śā 1.18-21); unconscious though active (Śā 1.75); in Bhela located between head and palate (Ci 8).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Bhela): citta rests in the heart and is the cause of all cognitions and actions; those of good citta go the good path (Bhela Ci 8).

literal: offence against (one's own) wisdom; failure of discernment

definitions.definition: The inauspicious act of body, speech or mind done by one whose intellect (dhī), resolve (dhṛti) and memory (smṛti) have lapsed; the provoker of all doṣas (Ca Śā 1.102); wrong knowing and wrong acting of the intellect (Śā 1.109); one of the three causes of disease (Sū 11.43); the source of adharma and so of epidemics (Vi 3.20) and the cause of exogenous insanity (Ni 7.10); all mental disorders are born of it (Sū 7.52).

equivalents.note: both name a root error of understanding behind suffering; prajñāparādha is an act (karma) proceeding from lapsed intellect, not a cosmic ignorance

literal: unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects

definitions.definition: Excessive, deficient or wrong contact of the senses with their objects, one of the three causes of disease (Ca Sū 11.37-38, 11.43; Śā 1.118-128).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): time, marked by the seasons, called 'transformation'; excessive, deficient or contrary seasons are the third cause of disease (Ca Sū 11.42-43); in Suśruta one of the candidate 'sources' (Su Śā 1.11).
The three supports of the body — food, sleep and continence — by which, rightly used, it continues strong for its full span (Ca Sū 11.35); 'as a house by its pillars' (AHS Sū 7.52).

The first support of life; wholesome food alone makes the person grow and unwholesome food causes disease (Ca Sū 25.31); its rule has eight factors (Vi 1.21); food is the root of living beings, of strength, complexion and ojas (Su Sū 1.28).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one of the three supports; one sleeps when the tired mind and senses withdraw from their objects; happiness, strength, knowledge and life depend on it (Ca Sū 21.35-36); seven kinds, of which night-born sleep is the 'nurse of beings' and tamas-born sleep the root of sin (Sū 21.58-59).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the third support of life (Ca Sū 11.35); 'the best of paths' (Sū 30.15); among the qualities of good conduct (Sū 8.29) and of the one who lives on constant rasāyana (Ci 1.4.30); required of the initiated medical student (Vi 8.13).
The daily regimen of the healthy: rising at the brāhma muhūrta, cleansing, collyrium, nasal oil, gargling, oil massage, exercise, bathing, conduct and timely sleep (AHS Sū 2; Ca Sū 5; Su Ci 24).
Regimen by season: the six seasons in the 'taking' (ādāna) and 'releasing' (visarga) halves of the year, with diet and conduct to suit the strength and doṣas of each (Ca Sū 6; AHS Sū 3).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the year has six seasons of two months each from Māgha — śiśira, vasanta, grīṣma, varṣā, śarad, hemanta (AHS Sū 3.1; Ca Sū 6.4).
The sun's northern course (late winter to summer) which takes away the earth's moisture and men's strength; fiery (Ca Sū 6.4-6; AHS Sū 3.2-4).
The sun's southern course (rains to early winter) in which the moon is strong and strength is given back; cool (Ca Sū 6.4-7; AHS Sū 3.4-6).

notes: Homonym: visarga is also the aspirate sign and, in the Purāṇas, secondary creation.

definitions.definition: The conduct of the good, to be followed always with mindfulness; it yields health and mastery of the senses at once (Ca Sū 8.17-18); it includes worship, cleanliness, truthful and gentle speech, non-covetousness, avoiding bad company and being devoted to continence, knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity and calm (Sū 8.18-29; AHS Sū 2.20-47).

The whole regimen by which the healthy keep their health — measure in food, daily and seasonal routine, urges, exercise and good conduct; one who follows it lives a hundred years free of disease (Ca Sū 8.31; 11.4).
One whose doṣas, fire, tissues, wastes and functions are balanced and whose self, senses and mind are clear (Su Sū 15.41).

Natural urges (of urine, faeces, semen, flatus, vomiting, sneezing, belching, yawning, hunger, thirst, tears, sleep, breath after exertion) which must not be suppressed; and the urges of greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, envy, passion and rash acts which must be restrained (Ca Sū 7.3-4, 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.1, 4.24).
Daily oil-massage of body, head, ears and feet, which makes the body firm, calms vāta and delays ageing (Ca Sū 5.81-92; AHS Sū 2.8-9).
Bodily exertion for steadiness and strength, to be done in measure (to half one's strength); excess causes disease (Ca Sū 7.31-35; AHS Sū 2.10-14).

literal: what has become one's own; suitability

definitions.definition: That which, used continuously, agrees with a person (Ca Vi 8.118); the unsuitable is 'what does not become one with the self' (Śā 1.127); changes of habit are to be made gradually (Sū 7.36-38).
Wholesome diet and conduct: that which keeps the balanced tissues balanced and restores the unbalanced (Ca Sū 25.33).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the branch and the means by which the healthy gain long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength — 'the means of obtaining the excellent rasa and other tissues' (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); taken by the hut-entering or the wind-and-sun mode (Ci 1.1.16); useless in an unpurified body (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4).
In Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (restricted), the fourth section of the Rasaratnākara 'for the aged' (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).

The name later given to Caraka's teaching that the truthful, non-angry, non-violent, calm, generous, devout and self-controlled person 'enjoys constant rasāyana' and alone gains the full benefits of rasāyana (Ca Ci 1.4.30-35; AHS Utt 39.179-181: 'nityarasāyana').

notes: The compound ācāra-rasāyana is the later name; the texts say 'nitya-rasāyana'.

definitions.definition: Rejuvenatives that promote the intellect — maṇḍūkaparṇī, liquorice, guḍūcī and above all śaṅkhapuṣpī (Ca Ci 1.3.30-31).

The principal and most difficult mode of rasāyana, taken in a specially built three-chambered hut after purification (Ca Ci 1.1.16-24, 1.4.27-28; AHS Utt 39.5-8); contrasted with vātātapika, taken amid ordinary life exposed to wind and sun.
The easier mode of rasāyana, taken without withdrawing from ordinary life (Ca Ci 1.1.16; 1.4.28).

The branch of virilization: that which gives offspring and delight and keeps semen fruitful into age, for the continuity of lineage here and endlessness hereafter (Ca Ci 1.1.9-12; Su Sū 1.8). Summary only.
The third kind of therapy: restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects (Ca Sū 11.54); its means are knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Sū 1.58).
Mantra, herbs worn, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, gifts, oblations, observances, expiation, fasting, benedictions, prostration and pilgrimage (Ca Sū 11.54; Vi 8.87).
The planned use of diet and medicines (Ca Sū 11.54): purification and pacification (Vi 8.87).

The five purificatory therapies — emesis, purgation, the two kinds of enema (decoction and oil), and nasal evacuation (bloodletting is counted instead by the surgeons) — preceded by oleation and sudation; the best medicines for the bodily doṣas (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 2, Si). Summary only.
Therapeutic emesis, the chief remedy for kapha (AHS Sū 1.25).
Therapeutic purgation, the chief remedy for pitta (AHS Sū 1.25).
Medicated enema (decoction or oil), the chief remedy for vāta (AHS Sū 1.25; Ca Sū 25.40 'best of vāta-removers').
Medication through the nose for the head; a daily practice in small measure (AHS Sū 2.6).
Bloodletting, counted by the surgical school among the purificatory therapies. Summary only.
Internal and external oiling, preparatory to purification and a therapy for vāta.
Inducing sweat, preparatory to purification; thirteen kinds with fire and ten without (Ca Sū 14).
Therapy that expels the doṣas (the pañcakarma); doṣas purified by it do not return, whereas those merely subdued may flare again (AHS Sū 4.26; Su Sū 1.27).
Therapy that pacifies the doṣas in place (by fasting, digestives, diet and medicines) without expelling them (Su Sū 1.27; AHS Sū 1.25 'śamana').
Lightening therapy — fasting, digestives, exercise and the like — against heaviness and excess; opposed to bṛṃhaṇa (Ca Sū 22).

notes: Ca Sū 22 not in the DCS portion checked; from memory. Prolonged fasting is not taught as a practice here.

definitions.definition: Nourishing therapy against emaciation and depletion (Ca Sū 22).
Āyurveda as knowledge of cause (hetu), sign (liṅga) and remedy (auṣadha), for the healthy and the sick; eternal (Ca Sū 1.24).
The effect sought and the purpose of the tantra (Ca Sū 1.53); health (Sū 9.4).
The four pillars of treatment — physician, medicine, attendant, patient — each with four qualities (Ca Sū 9.3-9; AHS Sū 1.27).
The three desires to be pursued: for life, for wealth and for the other world (Ca Sū 11.3).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): innate, seasonal/age-born and acquired (Ca Sū 11.36); identified with ojas (Su Sū 15.19).
The body's capacity to withstand disease: not all unwholesome things are equally harmful, nor all doṣas equally strong, nor all bodies equally able to resist disease (Ca Sū 28.7).

literal: sap; taste; essence; (in Rasa Śāstra) mercury

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) taste, the object of the tongue, sixfold — sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.64-65; 26.9); (2) the first tissue (AHS Sū 1.13).
In Rasa Śāstra, mercury, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.36); rasa as the means of crossing saṃsāra, identified with brahman ('raso vai saḥ', SDS Raseśvara 49).

notes: Homonym: in aesthetics and bhakti the relished sentiment.

definitions.definition: One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
One of the six tastes (Ca Sū 1.65; AHS Sū 1.14); for which doṣas it pacifies or provokes see Ca Sū 1.66.
The active potency of a substance, twofold as hot or cold (AHS Sū 1.17).
The taste a substance takes after digestion, threefold: sweet, sour, pungent (AHS Sū 1.17).
The specific action of a substance not explained by its taste, potency or vipāka (Ca Sū 26).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the twenty qualities in ten opposed pairs — heavy/light, cold/hot, unctuous/dry, slow/sharp, stable/mobile, soft/hard, clear/slimy, smooth/rough, subtle/gross, dense/liquid (Ca Sū 25.36; AHS Sū 1.18); the qualities as a category (Ca Sū 1.49); and the three guṇas of the mind (Śā 4.36).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the nine substances — five elements, self, mind, time, directions; with senses conscious, without them unconscious (Ca Sū 1.48); the inherent cause in which qualities and action reside (Sū 1.51); every substance is made of the five elements, and nothing in the world is not a medicine when rightly used (Sū 26.10-12).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the cause of increase — like increases like; it makes for oneness (Ca Sū 1.44-45).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the cause of decrease — the unlike reduces; it makes for separateness (Ca Sū 1.44-45).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): (1) action as a category — movement, the cause of conjunction and disjunction (Ca Sū 1.49, 1.52); (2) the deed of a former body, called daiva, whose fruit is this life (Sū 11.31; Vi 3.30); karma-born diseases subside only with its exhaustion (Śā 1.116-117); (3) the five purificatory acts.
The cause of disease, the first of the five means of knowing it; synonyms occasion, cause, basis, condition, origin (Mādhava Nidāna 1.4-5).
The unmanifest sign of an impending disease (Mādhava Nidāna 1.5-6).
The agreeable effect of medicine, food or conduct used contrary to the cause or the disease; it is sātmya (Mādhava Nidāna 1.8-9).
The way the disease comes into being by the vitiated, spreading doṣa (Mādhava Nidāna 1.10).
The six stages of a disease at each of which treatment may intervene — accumulation, provocation, spreading, lodging, manifestation, differentiation (Su Sū 21.18-36).
Signs appearing without cause that show the measure of life and approaching death, taught in the Indriyasthāna (Ca In 1.7; Sū 30.25).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): a synonym of srotas (Ca Vi 5.7); in Śārṅgadhara the pulse-vessel at the root of the thumb, 'witness of life' (Pūrva 3.1).

Diagnosis by the gait of the pulse — leech or snake for vāta, sparrow, crow or frog for pitta, swan or pigeon for kapha (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 3.1-5); absent from the classical saṃhitās' lists of examinations.
The eightfold excellence of the tissues (skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, mind) by which a physician judges strength, not by body-size (Ca Vi 8.102-115).
The devices of exposition by which a treatise is understood — thirty-six in Caraka (Si 12.41-45), thirty-two in Suśruta (Utt 65.3).
Discussion among physicians, friendly or hostile (Ca Vi 8.15-23).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): disputation with another based on the science, of two kinds, jalpa and vitaṇḍā (Ca Vi 8.28).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): each party establishing its own thesis and attacking the other's, e.g. 'rebirth exists' against 'it does not' (Ca Vi 8.28).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): merely finding fault with the other side (Ca Vi 8.28).

Caraka's fourth means of knowledge: the understanding that sees things produced by the conjunction of many causes, valid for the three times, by which the three aims are achieved (Ca Sū 11.25); also the right application of medicine to place, time and person (Sū 1.123-127).
The word of those freed from rajas and tamas, whose knowledge of the three times is pure — the Veda and teachings not contrary to it (Ca Sū 11.18-19, 11.27; Vi 4.4).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the supreme self is changeless, eternal, the cause of consciousness with mind, elements and senses, the seer (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the knower of the field, all-pervading, witness, known by the marks of life (breath, blinking, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, memory, ego-sense) (Śā 1.59-85); knows only through its instruments (Śā 1.54-55).
Suśruta: the knowers of the field in Āyurveda are eternal but not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.16).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the conjunction of mind, self and body, subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.47); the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Śā 1.16-17); 'the measure of the world' (Śā 5.3); in Suśruta the union of the five elements and the embodied one (Su Sū 1.22).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the unmanifest self, knower of the field of the twenty-three (Ca Śā 1.61-65); for Suśruta many, eternal, not all-pervading (Su Śā 1.3, 1.16).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka the self as knower of the field, and one of the eightfold prakṛti (Śā 1.61-63); in Suśruta the uncaused cause of all beings, threefold in guṇas, support of many knowers of the field (Su Śā 1.3).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the inner self of the embryo, eternal, unaging, deathless, that enters the womb through its connection with mind and 'produces itself' as the embryo (Ca Śā 3.3, 3.8).
The empirical person, the aggregate of twenty-four, born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma, in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain are established (Ca Śā 1.35-37, 1.53).
The final cure, without upadhā, which ends suffering altogether — renunciation of all grasping (Ca Śā 1.94-95); 'naiṣṭhikī' also qualifies the true understanding in Śā 5.26.

literal: grasping; craving as the basis of suffering

definitions.definition: The supreme cause giving suffering and the seats of suffering; its total renunciation removes all suffering (Ca Śā 1.95).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): craving consisting of desire and aversion arises from pleasure and pain and is again their cause, grasping the seats of feeling (Ca Śā 1.134-135); the ignorant takes it from objects as the silkworm its deadly threads (Śā 1.96).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the complete cessation of all feeling (Śā 1.137); separation from all conjunctions through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma — non-return (Śā 1.142); disengagement (nivṛtti), the supreme, tranquil, imperishable brahman (Śā 5.11).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda, Caraka): the state in which, the mind being steady and established in the self, pleasure and pain cease and mastery arises in the embodied — it leads to liberation (Śā 1.137-139); its eight powers (Śā 1.140-141); also 'yoga' = right combination/application of drugs (Sū 1.123).
The liberated self after the final renunciation, no longer perceived, without mark (Ca Śā 1.155; 5.21).
The understanding 'this is not I, this is not mine' (Ca Śā 1.153), arising in one who sees the world in himself and himself in the world (Śā 5.7).
The presence of the memory of truth from which all the means of liberation proceed; 'the one path shown by the liberated' (Ca Śā 1.146-150).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): memory arising from eight causes (Ca Śā 1.148-149); its lapse regarding truth is a cause of suffering (Śā 1.101); good conduct is to be followed 'with smṛti' (Sū 8.17); constant present mindfulness (saṃnihita-smṛti) guards from suffering (AHS Sū 2.47).
The discerning intellect whose lapse — seeing the eternal and non-eternal, wholesome and unwholesome wrongly — is a cause of suffering (Ca Śā 1.99).
The restraining resolve whose lapse leaves the mind unable to turn from the harmful (Ca Śā 1.100); with smṛti and dhī the means of stopping the stream of body and mind (Śā 2.42).
Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): one's own deed of a former body (Ca Vi 3.30; Śā 1.116; 2.44); balanced against present effort (Vi 3.29-36).
What is done here in this life, which can overcome a weak daiva (Ca Vi 3.30-33).
Death before the exhaustion of life's measure through wrong conduct, as an axle breaks midway (Ca Vi 3.38; Śā 6.28).
Simultaneous disease of many through vitiated air, water, land and season, whose root is adharma arising from prajñāparādha (Ca Vi 3.6-23).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): a seizing being — of eight classes: gods, their enemies, gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas, piśācas — whose seizure shows as superhuman knowledge and action (Su Utt 60.4-7); the subject of bhūtavidyā. Summary only.
Derangement of mind, fivefold (from each doṣa, all three, and exogenous); the exogenous kind is caused by prajñāparādha and treated by the divine therapies (Ca Ni 7.10-17).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): dreams are sevenfold — of what was seen, heard, experienced, desired, imagined, portending, and born of doṣas (Ca In 5.43); in Ca Sū 11.35 'svapna' = sleep as a support.
The science of processing mercury and minerals for the body's stability, jīvanmukti and medicine; also rasavidyā, rasatantra (Rasārṇava 1.46; SDS Raseśvara 23).

Mercury, so called because it gives the far shore (pāra) of saṃsāra (SDS Raseśvara 1-2), or because adepts proclaim it for others (para-artha) (Rasārṇava 1.35); Śiva's seed (harabīja), also called rasa, sūta, rasendra, rasarāja (Rasārṇava 1.28, 1.34-36).
Mica, the seed of Gaurī (the Goddess), joined with mercury (Śiva's seed) to make the divine body (SDS Raseśvara 9-10).
Sulphur, used with mercury in rasa medicine; impure sulphur is said to cause severe skin disease, burning and giddiness (Rasaratnākara, Rasakhaṇḍa 5.4).

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra / later Āyurveda): the calcined preparation of a metal, mineral or gem used as medicine; the texts insist that only properly purified and processed material is used, the impure being life-destroying (RRS 5.47-48, 5.73). RESTRICTED: no processes recorded.

notes: Homonym: sacred ash of the Śaiva ascetics.

definitions.definition: The transformation of the body by mercury, the supreme purpose of rasa-śāstra, leading to the sky-going state (SDS Raseśvara 23-24).
The transmutation of metals by mercury, to be tested first before application to the body (SDS Raseśvara 24-25).
Metallurgical alchemy; rasa-śāstra is not merely for this (SDS Raseśvara 23); the 'vāda-khaṇḍa' of the Rasaratnākara is for alchemists (vādin) (Rasakhaṇḍa 1.5).
The eighteen processings of mercury required before it can be used; named in the SDS (Raseśvara 19-21) and detailed in the rasa texts. RESTRICTED: names and procedures not recorded.

notes: Homonym: saṃskāra as latent impression and as life-cycle rite.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): purification of mercury and minerals to remove their inherent impurities, without which mercury is poison (Rasaratnākara, Rasakhaṇḍa 1.30). RESTRICTED: no procedure recorded.
In Āyurveda: purification therapy (saṃśodhana), see trm:samsodhana.
Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): the seven adventitious 'coverings' (impurities) of mercury, from earth, rock and water, causing skin disease, dullness and wind disorders (RRS 11.22-25).

notes: Homonym: in Kashmir Śaivism the (five/six) 'coverings' limiting consciousness.

definitions.definition: The firmness of the body, the precondition of jīvanmukti in the rasa doctrine (SDS Raseśvara 1; Rasārṇava 1.11, 1.18).

The body 'born of the creation of Hara and Gaurī' (mercury and mica), permanent though the six-sheathed body is not; to be produced first by the yogin seeking jīvanmukti (SDS Raseśvara 7-9; Rasahṛdaya 1.7).

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8); attained through the stable body made by mercury, not after the body falls (Rasārṇava 1.9-13; SDS Raseśvara 1-5).
The power of sky-going given by 'bound' mercury and bound breath (Rasārṇava 1.19), and the aim of dehavedha (SDS Raseśvara 24).
Those who, without abandoning the body, have gained the body born of Hara and Gaurī, whose servants are the mantras (Rasahṛdaya 1.7); twenty-seven are listed in RRS 1.2-5.
A liṅga made of processed mercury, whose worship is praised above that of all other liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.43; RRS 1.24, 6.19). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.
The hall for rasa work in a safe, righteous land, spacious and well provided with windows, with a secluded rasa-pavilion beside it (RRS 6.11-14).
Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): until śaktipāta and the cutting of the fetters, understanding of mercury does not arise (Rasārṇava 1.23).

The three states of processed mercury in the doctrine: swooned it removes disease, 'dead' it revives, bound it gives sky-going (Rasārṇava 1.19; Rasahṛdaya 1.3); the same said of breath. RESTRICTED: the tests and processes are not recorded.
